## Problem 1

I selected `Petal.Length` as the classification feature because it provides better separation among the three iris species.

```{r do1, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(ggbeeswarm)

ggplot(pivot_longer(iris, cols=1:4),
       aes(x=factor(name), y=value, colour=Species)) +
  geom_beeswarm()
```

I used thresholds of 2.5 and 4.9 to classify the samples into three groups.

```{r lkdisc}
feature = "Petal.Length"
cutsl = c(0, 2.5, 4.9, 7)

with(iris, table(cut(Petal.Length, cutsl), Species))
```

These thresholds completely separate setosa from the other two species. Most versicolor and virginica samples are also correctly classified. The confusion matrix contains 8 off-diagonal observations, meaning that 142 out of 150 samples are correctly classified.

## Problem 2

I fitted a two-parameter linear regression model using maternal body weight (`lwt`) to predict the low birth weight outcome (`low`).

```{r lklbw, message=FALSE}
library(MASS)

fit = lm(low ~ lwt, data = birthwt)

summary(fit)

predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(lwt = 150))
```

The model has two parameters: an intercept and a slope for maternal body weight. Since `low` is a binary variable, the fitted value can be interpreted as the estimated proportion of births with low birth weight outcomes.

The estimated proportion for women weighing 150 pounds is:

```{r}
estimated_proportion = predict(
  fit,
  newdata = data.frame(lwt = 150)
)

cat("Estimated proportion:",
    round(estimated_proportion, 4))
```
